item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports separating recommendation relevance from preference elicitation and decision outcomes. PEPPER (2025) identifies target ambiguity and limitations of single-turn target recall; a 2026 evaluation study examines whether offline model rankings agree with dense relevance judgments ([PEPPER](https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-emnlp.1067/), [convergent validity](https://mdw.ekstrandom.net/pubs/recsys26-eval)). Practical synthesis: annotate specific attribute matches separately from broad topical relevance; distinguish immediate choice, deferral, explicit rejection, and inability to identify an item. Record redundancy through identifiable repeated items or overlapping attributes. Attach title/description evidence spans to each attribute claim; mark compatibility, ownership, current intent, and simulator traits unknown unless explicitly supported. These are proposed audit rules, not validated labels established by those studies.\n\nPreference pairs need their own reliability audit. ICLR 2024 research found substantial disagreement between preferences elicited through ratings and rankings, so a higher relevance rating should not automatically become an A-over-B preference ([feedback protocols](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/48a4f41ff000b121eabe7b2491b24aef-Abstract-Conference.html)). Preserve the original feedback, comparison context, evidence, and labels for ties or insufficient information; reverse pair order to check sensitivity. Position-bias research supports checking presentation effects, while abstention research shows models can struggle to withhold unsupported answers ([position bias](https://aclanthology.org/2025.ijcnlp-long.18/), [abstention](https://aclanthology.org/2025.coling-main.627/)). Recommended checks: independently double-annotate a sample, report agreement and label counts, adjudicate disagreements, and retain unknowns. Missing metadata is an evidence limitation, not evidence of dislike."}
